source.basis: Operator facility page; structured facts only, no operator prose reproduced.

reading.body:
A single 114 MW campus in Sterling, Virginia accounts for 7.1 percent of the state's published data center capacity and ranks third among the 25 Virginia facilities that disclose a megawatt figure.

The more useful number is the one that is missing. Virginia has 330 mapped data centers and published capacity for only 25 of them, so the 1,603 MW state total is a floor rather than a measurement. Any share calculated against it, including this facility's 7.1 percent, is a share of disclosure, not of the state's actual load. The true figure is substantially larger and the data does not say by how much.

For AI specifically, 114 MW is a meaningful unit of compute. At an assumed 400 watts per rack and 8 accelerators per rack, the campus supports roughly 285 racks and about 2,280 high-end GPUs. That estimate rests on two assumptions the data does not verify, and it describes a building's power envelope rather than its actual workload. The 685,000 square feet of technical space is not the constraint. Power is.

What the data does not cover matters as much as what it does. It says nothing about grid interconnection status, expansion limits in Northern Virginia, or whether this capacity is contracted to AI training, AI serving, or something else entirely. It also does not establish that the facility is the largest of its kind, only that it is smaller than the largest US campuses. The LEED certification speaks to environmental management of operations, not to the carbon intensity of the power delivered.
